summary.text: Couple the evolutions from masses \(n\) and \(n+1\): at every time their configurations differ by one extra unit, while every reachable configuration is a prefix of unit cells followed by masses at least two and at most one final unit cell. This shape invariant shows that once the smaller system is stable the larger stabilizes within two more steps, whereas if the larger stabilizes on its next step then the smaller was already stable, giving \(a(n)<a(n+1)\le a(n)+2\).

full_proof.text:
Let a configuration be a finite list of nonnegative integers, read from left to right. We write
\[
\left\lceil \frac{x}{2}\right\rceil=\frac{x+1}{2},\qquad
\left\lfloor \frac{x}{2}\right\rfloor=\frac{x}{2},
\]
where the expressions on the right use integer division.

It is convenient first to give a recursive description of one update. For an integer \(b\ge 0\) and a list \(L\), define \(F_b(L)\) by
\[
F_b([])=
\begin{cases}
[],&b=0,\\
[b],&b>0,
\end{cases}
\]
and
\[
F_b(x::X)=\left(\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil+b\right)::F_{\lfloor x/2\rfloor}(X).
\]
Here \(b\) represents mass received from the cell immediately to the left. Thus the cellular-automaton update is
\[
T(L)=F_0(L).
\]
For \(t\ge0\), let
\[
R(n,t)=T^t([n]).
\]

We will prove that the sequence in the question is precisely the least \(t\) for which
\[
R(n,t)=[1,1,\ldots,1]
\]
with \(n\) entries, and then compare the runs with initial masses \(n\) and \(n+1\).

First we record some elementary properties of \(F_b\).

1. If every entry of \(L\) is positive, then every entry of \(F_b(L)\) is positive. Indeed, for a nonempty input the first output is
\(\lceil x/2\rceil+b\ge1\), and the assertion for the remaining entries follows recursively. If the input is empty, the output is either empty or the one-element positive list \([b]\).

2. Mass is conserved, including the incoming mass:
\[
\sum F_b(L)=b+\sum L.
\]
This follows by induction on \(L\). For \(L=[]\) it is immediate. For \(L=x::X\), use the induction hypothesis with incoming mass \(\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), together with
\[
\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil+
\left\lfloor\frac{x}{2}\right\rfloor=x.
\]
In particular, \(T\) preserves total mass.

3. A leading cell of mass one remains fixed and has no effect on the rest:
\[
T(1::X)=1::T(X).
\]
Consequently,
\[
T^t(1::X)=1::T^t(X)
\]
for every \(t\).

We next prove that every positive configuration eventually stabilizes. More precisely, every finite list \(L\) of positive integers and total mass \(N\) eventually becomes the list \(1^N\) of \(N\) ones.

We use strong induction on the total mass \(N\), and, for a nonempty list \(x::X\), a nested strong induction on its first entry \(x\). If \(L=[]\), then \(N=0\), and it is already \(1^0=[]\). Suppose now that \(L=x::X\).

If \(x=1\), then \(X\) has total mass \(N-1<N\). By the outer induction hypothesis, some iterate of \(X\) is \(1^{N-1}\). Since a leading one remains fixed under every update, the same number of updates sends \(1::X\) to \(1^N\).

If \(x>1\), make one update. The resulting list is
\[
\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil::F_{\lfloor x/2\rfloor}(X).
\]
It is positive, has the same total mass \(N\), and its first entry satisfies
\[
1\le \left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil<x.
\]
The inner strong induction hypothesis therefore applies to this new list and shows that it eventually becomes \(1^N\). Thus the original list does so one step earlier. This proves convergence.

We now introduce the coupling between configurations whose total masses differ by one. Say that \(E(X,Y)\) holds if \(Y\) is obtained from \(X\) by adding one unit to exactly one existing entry, or by appending a new final entry equal to one. Recursively, this means:

- \(E([],[1])\);
- \(E(x::X,(x+1)::X)\);
- if \(E(X,Y)\), then \(E(x::X,x::Y)\).

This relation has several immediate properties. The second list is never empty. If \(X\) is positive and \(E(X,Y)\), then \(Y\) is positive. Also, it always increases total mass by one.

The crucial coupling fact is that the update preserves \(E\): for every \(b\),
\[
E(X,Y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E(F_b(X),F_b(Y)). \tag{1}
\]
We prove this by induction on the position of the extra unit. Two simple observations account for the only nontrivial case.

First, increasing the incoming mass from \(b\) to \(b+1\) inserts exactly one extra unit into the output:
\[
E(F_b(X),F_{b+1}(X)). \tag{2}
\]
If \(X=[]\), this is checked directly: when \(b=0\), the pair is \(([],[1])\), and when \(b>0\), it is \(([b],[b+1])\). If \(X\ne[]\), only the first output entry increases by one.

Now suppose the extra unit is in the first input cell, so that the first entries are \(x\) and \(x+1\). If \(x\) is even, then increasing \(x\) by one increases the retained amount \(\lceil x/2\rceil\) by one and leaves the forwarded amount \(\lfloor x/2\rfloor\) unchanged. Thus the extra unit appears in the first output cell. If \(x\) is odd, the retained amount is unchanged and the forwarded amount increases by one; then (2) shows that the two output tails satisfy \(E\). If the extra input unit lies farther to the right, the first output cells agree and induction applies to the tails. The append-at-the-end case is included in the same recursion. This proves (1).

Since \(E([n],[n+1])\), repeated use of (1) gives
\[
E(R(n,t),R(n+1,t)) \qquad\text{for every }t. \tag{3}
\]

For the upper bound on the difference of stabilization times, we need a shape invariant. Call a list a core if it is one of the following:

- the empty list;
- the one-element list \([1]\);
- a list \(x::X\) with \(x\ge2\) and \(X\) a core.

Thus a core consists of entries at least two, possibly followed by one single final one. Call a list nice if it consists of any number of leading ones followed by a core. Equivalently, a nice list has the form
\[
1^r::C,
\]
where \(C\) is a core.

Every positive one-cell initial configuration \([n]\) is nice: it is \([1]\) when \(n=1\), and otherwise is a core whose sole entry is at least two. We claim that niceness is preserved by \(T\).

It suffices first to understand what happens to a core when it receives a positive incoming mass. If \(C\) is a core and \(b\ge1\), then
\[
F_b(C)
\]
is again a core. This is proved by induction on \(C\). If \(C=[]\), the output is \([b]\), which is \([1]\) if \(b=1\) and otherwise has an entry at least two. If \(C=[1]\), the output is \([b+1]\), whose entry is at least two. Finally, if \(C=x::X\) with \(x\ge2\), then the first output entry is
\[
\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil+b\ge2,
\]
and the tail is \(F_{\lfloor x/2\rfloor}(X)\). Since \(x\ge2\), the incoming mass \(\lfloor x/2\rfloor\) for the tail is at least one, so induction shows that this tail is a core.

Now apply \(T\) to a nice list. Every leading one stays a leading one, so it remains only to consider a core. The empty core and \([1]\) remain nice. If the core begins with \(x\ge2\), then
\[
T(x::X)=\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil::F_{\lfloor x/2\rfloor}(X).
\]
The tail is a core by the preceding paragraph. The first output is either one, in which case it is a new leading one before that core, or is at least two, in which case the entire output is a core. Hence \(T\) preserves niceness. It follows that
\[
R(n,t)\text{ is nice for every }n\ge1\text{ and every }t. \tag{4}
\]

We next prove the key two-step lemma:

> If \(E(1^n,Y)\) and \(Y\) is nice, then
> \[
> T^2(Y)=1^{n+1}. \tag{5}
> \]

The relation \(E(1^n,Y)\) says that \(Y\) is obtained either by appending a final one, or by changing one of the entries of \(1^n\) from one to two. In the former case \(Y=1^{n+1}\), so it is already stable and remains so.

In the latter case, write
\[
Y=1^r::2::1^s,
\qquad r+s+1=n.
\]
Niceness forces \(s\le1\). Indeed, after the leading prefix \(1^r\), the list \(2::1^s\) must be a core. But a core may have at most one final entry equal to one, so two or more ones cannot follow the two.

It therefore suffices, after ignoring the fixed leading prefix, to check two cases. If \(s=0\), then
\[
T([2])=[1,1],

a stable list. If \(s=1\), then
\[
T([2,1])=[1,2],
\qquad
T([1,2])=[1,1,1].
\]
Thus in either case at most two updates produce the appropriate all-ones list. Reattaching the unchanged leading ones proves (5).

We also need a converse-type fact to obtain strict growth of the stabilization time. We first note the following simple lemma:

> If \(X\) is positive, \(b\ge1\), and every entry of \(F_b(X)\) equals one, then \(X=[]\). \tag{6}

For if \(X=x::X'\) were nonempty, then its first output would be
\[
\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil+b\ge1+1=2,
\]
contrary to the assumption that all output entries are one.

Now suppose
\[
E(X,Y),
\]
\(X\) is positive, and every entry of \(T(Y)\) equals one. We claim that every entry of \(X\) already equals one. We prove this by following the recursive definition of \(E\).

If \(X=[]\) and \(Y=[1]\), the conclusion is immediate. Suppose the extra unit occurs at the first position:
\[
X=x::X',\qquad Y=(x+1)::X'.
\]
The first entry of \(T(Y)\) is \(\lceil(x+1)/2\rceil\), and it equals one. Positivity of \(x\) then forces \(x=1\). The tail of \(T(Y)\) is consequently \(F_1(X')\), all of whose entries are one. By (6), \(X'=[]\). Hence \(X=[1]\).

Finally suppose the first entries agree:
\[
X=x::X',\qquad Y=x::Y',\qquad E(X',Y').
\]
The first entry of \(T(Y)\) is \(\lceil x/2\rceil=1\). Since \(x>0\), this gives \(x=1\) or \(x=2\).

If \(x=1\), the tail of \(T(Y)\) is \(T(Y')\), and it consists entirely of ones. By induction, every entry of \(X'\) is one, so every entry of \(X\) is one.

If \(x=2\), the tail of \(T(Y)\) is \(F_1(Y')\), all of whose entries are one. The list \(Y'\) is positive because \(X'\) is positive and \(E(X',Y')\). Lemma (6) therefore gives \(Y'=[]\). But this is impossible: whenever \(E(X',Y')\), the second list \(Y'\) is nonempty. Thus the case \(x=2\) cannot occur. We have proved
\[
E(X,Y),\ X\text{ positive},\ T(Y)\text{ all ones}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X\text{ all ones}. \tag{7}
\]

We now connect this argument exactly to the update used in the definition of \(a(n)\). Given a list \(L=[x_1,\ldots,x_k]\), the original update forms the two lists
\[
\left[\left\lceil\frac{x_1}{2}\right\rceil,
\ldots,
\left\lceil\frac{x_k}{2}\right\rceil,0\right]

a nd
\[
\left[0,
\left\lfloor\frac{x_1}{2}\right\rfloor,
\ldots,
\left\lfloor\frac{x_k}{2}\right\rfloor\right],
\]
adds them coordinatewise, and removes trailing zeros. More generally, replacing the initial zero in the second list by \(b\) gives a raw list satisfying the recursion
\[
\operatorname{Raw}_b([])=[b],
\]
\[
\operatorname{Raw}_b(x::X)=
\left(\left\lceil\frac{x}{2}\right\rceil+b\right)::
\operatorname{Raw}_{\lfloor x/2\rfloor}(X).
\]
If \(L\) is positive, every nonfinal entry displayed by this recursion is positive. Removing trailing zeros therefore gives exactly \(F_b(L)\): in the empty case it removes \([0]\) when \(b=0\), and otherwise retains \([b]\); in the nonempty case the positive first entry is retained and the same assertion applies recursively to the tail. Thus, on every positive configuration, the original update is exactly \(T=F_0\).

Starting from \([n]\) with \(n\ge1\), all later configurations are positive, as proved above. Hence the state after \(t\) original updates is precisely \(R(n,t)\). By convergence, the set
\[
\{t\in\mathbb N:R(n,t)=1^n\}
\]
is nonempty. Therefore its least element exists, belongs to the set, and is no larger than any other element of the set. This least element is exactly \(a(n)\). In particular,
\[
R(n,a(n))=1^n, \tag{8}
\]
and whenever \(R(n,t)=1^n\),
\[
a(n)\le t. \tag{9}
\]

We can now prove the two required bounds.

First, \(a(n+1)>a(n)\) for every \(n\ge1\). The number \(a(n+1)\) is positive, because at time zero the configuration is \([n+1]\), which is not the list \(1^{n+1}\) when \(n+1\ge2\). Write
\[
a(n+1)=t+1.
\]
At time \(t+1\), the larger run is stable by (8), so every entry of
\[
T(R(n+1,t))=R(n+1,t+1)
\]
is one. By (3),
\[
E(R(n,t),R(n+1,t)),
\]
and \(R(n,t)\) is positive. Applying (7), every entry of \(R(n,t)\) is one. Its total mass is \(n\), so it must be exactly \(1^n\). By (9), \(a(n)\le t\). Therefore
\[
a(n)<t+1=a(n+1). \tag{10}
\]

Second, \(a(n+1)\le a(n)+2\). At time \(a(n)\), equation (8) and the coupling (3) give
\[
E(1^n,R(n+1,a(n))).
\]
By (4), the larger configuration \(R(n+1,a(n))\) is nice. The two-step lemma (5) therefore yields
\[
R(n+1,a(n)+2)=1^{n+1}.
\]
The minimality property (9) gives
\[
a(n+1)\le a(n)+2. \tag{11}
\]

Combining (10) and (11), \(a(n+1)\) is an integer strictly larger than \(a(n)\) but no larger than \(a(n)+2\). Hence for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
a(n+1)=a(n)+1
\quad\text{or}\quad
a(n+1)=a(n)+2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{1,2\},
\]
as claimed.
